body:
Mathematics in ancient Indian society

Mathematical knowledge developed in ancient India through practical activities such as measurement, construction, calculation and the study of celestial movements. Some of the earliest surviving mathematical rules appear in texts concerned with constructing ritual altars. Later scholars developed systematic methods of arithmetic, geometry and mathematical astronomy.

An important distinction is that these developments did not occur at one time or through one individual. The geometric rules associated with Baudhayana belong to a much earlier period than the mathematical and astronomical works of Aryabhata, Brahmagupta and Bhaskara.

Baudhayana and the Sulba Sutras

Baudhayana is associated with the Baudhayana Sulba Sutra, one of the earliest surviving Indian texts containing rules of practical geometry. Its composition is generally placed approximately between 800 BCE and 500 BCE, although Baudhayana's exact lifetime is unknown.

The word sulba means a cord or measuring rope, while sutra means a concise rule. The Sulba Sutras describe methods for laying out altars of specified shapes and sizes. A cord could be stretched to mark a straight line, measure a length or establish a geometric relationship.

The diagonal rule

A well-known rule associated with the Baudhayana Sulba Sutra expresses the relationship between the sides and diagonal of a rectangle. In modern mathematical language, it corresponds to the Pythagorean theorem: the square of the diagonal equals the sum of the squares of the 2 perpendicular sides.

For example, a rectangle measuring 3 units by 4 units has a diagonal of 5 units, because 32 + 42 = 52, or 9 + 16 = 25. This relationship allows a right angle to be checked during construction.

The text also gives a close approximation for the diagonal of a square. If the side of a square is 1 unit, its diagonal is approximately 1.4142 units. The exact mathematical value is the square root of 2.

The Sulba Sutras express geometrical knowledge through construction rules. Writing their relationships with modern algebraic symbols helps explain them, but those symbols were not used in the ancient text.

Why the contribution matters

The importance of the Sulba Sutras lies in their application of mathematical relationships to accurate measurement and construction. They demonstrate that geometrical knowledge existed in India long before the mathematical astronomy of the Gupta and post-Gupta periods.

Prelims focus

  • Baudhayana: early Indian geometry and altar construction.
  • Principal work: Baudhayana Sulba Sutra.
  • Approximate period: 800–500 BCE.
  • Sulba: measuring cord or rope.
  • Key mathematical idea: the relationship between the sides and diagonal of a rectangle.
  • Trap: Baudhayana's Sulba Sutra is not an astronomical work like Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya.

[Sources: National Mission for Manuscripts, History and Development of Mathematics in India, discussion of the Sulba Sutras, pp. 388–390; University of St Andrews, MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Baudhayana' and 'Indian Sulbasutras', consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Baudhayana and the Origins of Practical Geometry in India

body:
Aryabhata and the Aryabhatiya

Aryabhata I was an Indian mathematician and astronomer born around 476 CE. His principal surviving work, the Aryabhatiya, was completed in 499 CE. It was written in Sanskrit verse and combined mathematical methods with calculations concerning celestial movements.

Aryabhata is associated with Kusumapura, commonly connected with the region of Pataliputra, near present-day Patna in Bihar. The precise location of his birthplace is uncertain.

His work belongs to the period of the Gupta age and demonstrates the close relationship between mathematics and astronomy in ancient India. Calculating planetary positions, eclipses and astronomical periods required reliable methods of arithmetic, geometry and trigonometry.

Earth's rotation and the apparent movement of the Sun

Aryabhata explained that day and night result from Earth's rotation on its axis. Earth turns, causing different parts of its surface to face towards or away from the Sun.

To an observer standing on Earth, the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west. This apparent daily movement can be explained by Earth's rotation rather than by the Sun travelling around Earth each day.

This is different from Earth's revolution around the Sun, which is its orbital movement. A question about the immediate cause of day and night is testing rotation, not revolution.

Scientific explanation of eclipses

Aryabhata explained eclipses through the relative positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon, rather than treating them solely as supernatural events.

  • Solar eclipse: the Moon moves between the Sun and Earth and blocks sunlight from reaching part of Earth's surface.
  • Lunar eclipse: Earth moves between the Sun and Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

These are distinct alignments. A solar eclipse is associated with the new-moon phase, while a lunar eclipse is associated with the full-moon phase. An eclipse does not occur at every new or full moon because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane.

Mathematics in the Aryabhatiya

Aryabhata worked on mathematical problems involving numbers, measurement and the calculation of astronomical positions. His work includes methods of calculation and trigonometric relationships useful in astronomy.

One notable result is his close approximation of pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. His rule gives:

62832 ÷ 20000 = 3.1416.

This is very close to the modern value of pi, approximately 3.14159. The result matters because accurate calculations involving circles and angles were important for mathematical astronomy.

Aryabhata is especially associated with the Aryabhatiya, Earth's rotation, eclipses and mathematical astronomy. He should not be described as the sole inventor of zero; the Indian number system developed through several stages and contributions.

Prelims focus

  • Aryabhata I: mathematician and astronomer, born around 476 CE.
  • Aryabhatiya: completed in 499 CE.
  • Day and night: explained through Earth's rotation.
  • Eclipses: explained through celestial alignments and shadows.
  • Approximation of pi: 3.1416.
  • Trap: Earth's rotation and Earth's revolution are different movements.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, chapter 'Buildings, Paintings and Books', printed p. 131; University of St Andrews, MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Aryabhata the Elder', sections on the Aryabhatiya and mathematical astronomy, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Earth's rotation explains the succession of day and night.

title: Aryabhata: Mathematical Astronomy, Earth's Rotation and Eclipses

body:
Varahamihira and astronomical scholarship

Varahamihira was a mathematician, astronomer and astrologer of the 6th century CE, conventionally dated approximately 505–587 CE. He worked at Ujjain, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, an important centre of mathematical astronomy.

His significance lies partly in bringing together earlier astronomical traditions. Astronomers needed methods to calculate the positions of celestial bodies, predict eclipses and prepare calendars. Different texts offered different computational rules, and Varahamihira preserved and compared several of these systems.

Panchasiddhantika: the 5 astronomical systems

Varahamihira's most important astronomical work is the Panchasiddhantika, meaning a compendium of 5 astronomical doctrines. The work is generally dated to the 6th century CE.

It discusses the following traditions:

  • Surya or Saura Siddhanta
  • Romaka Siddhanta
  • Paulisa Siddhanta
  • Vasistha Siddhanta
  • Paitamaha Siddhanta

The Panchasiddhantika is therefore not simply another name for Aryabhata's work. Aryabhata composed the Aryabhatiya; Varahamihira brought together 5 astronomical systems in the Panchasiddhantika.

Brihat Samhita and related subjects

Another major work associated with Varahamihira is the Brihat Samhita. It is an extensive compilation covering celestial phenomena, weather-related observations and a range of other subjects. He is also associated with the Brihajjataka, a work on astrology.

Astronomy and astrology were often studied together in this historical setting, but they are not equivalent concepts. Astronomy concerns celestial bodies and their movements. Astrology assigns predictive meanings to celestial positions and is not established as a modern empirical science.

Match the author to the work: Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya, whereas Varahamihira wrote the Panchasiddhantika and the Brihat Samhita.

Prelims focus

  • Varahamihira: 6th-century mathematician and astronomer.
  • Associated centre: Ujjain.
  • Panchasiddhantika: compilation of 5 astronomical systems.
  • Brihat Samhita: encyclopaedic work including celestial and weather-related subjects.
  • Trap: Panchasiddhantika belongs to Varahamihira, not Brahmagupta.

[Sources: University of St Andrews, MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Varahamihira', sections on the Panchasiddhantika and Brihatsamhita, consulted 18 November 2026; National Mission for Manuscripts, Kriti Rakshana, June 2023, article 'Varahamihira and his Panchasiddhantika', discussion of the 5 siddhantas.]

pictures.caption: The 5 astronomical traditions discussed in the Panchasiddhantika.

title: Varahamihira and the Five Traditions of Indian Astronomy

body:
Decimal place value: why the position of a digit matters

The decimal place-value system represents numbers using the digits 0 to 9. It is called decimal because each place represents a power of 10: units, tens, hundreds, thousands and so on.

The value of a digit depends on its position. For example, the number 205 means 2 hundreds, 0 tens and 5 units. The number 25 means 2 tens and 5 units. These numbers are different because moving a digit to another place changes its value.

Zero has 2 related functions: it can act as a placeholder in a numeral, and it can be treated as a number in arithmetic. In 205, the digit 0 indicates that there are no tens. In the calculation 7 − 7 = 0, zero represents the result of subtracting a number from itself.

Why zero made calculations more systematic

Place-value notation allows large numbers to be written with relatively few symbols. A digit can represent different values according to its position, and the digit 0 preserves positions that contain no units of a particular order.

Indian mathematical traditions made important contributions to the development and systematic use of this notation. The numeral system was subsequently transmitted through the Arabic-speaking scholarly world and became widely used elsewhere.

The development of zero took place over time. It is therefore misleading to assign the invention of every aspect of the decimal system and zero to one named individual.

Brahmagupta and the Brahmasphutasiddhanta

Brahmagupta was a mathematician and astronomer who lived approximately from 598 CE to 670 CE. He composed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in 628 CE at Bhillamala, identified with present-day Bhinmal in Rajasthan. He is also associated with the important mathematical astronomy tradition of Ujjain.

His other significant work is the Khandakhadyaka, composed in 665 CE, which deals with astronomical calculations.

Rules involving zero and negative numbers

Brahmagupta gave systematic arithmetic rules involving zero, positive numbers and negative numbers. He described positive and negative quantities using terms comparable to fortunes and debts.

Several of his rules can be expressed in familiar modern notation:

  • Subtraction of equals: 7 − 7 = 0.
  • Adding zero: 7 + 0 = 7.
  • Multiplying by zero: 8 × 0 = 0.
  • Combining positive and negative numbers: 4 + (−6) = −2.
  • Multiplying 2 negative numbers: (−3) × (−2) = 6.

These rules were important because they treated zero and negative quantities within a systematic method of calculation.

The important exception: division by zero

Brahmagupta also attempted to explain division involving zero, but not all his conclusions were correct. In particular, his treatment of 0 divided by 0 does not agree with modern mathematics.

Division by zero is undefined in ordinary arithmetic. Neither 5 ÷ 0 nor 0 ÷ 0 has a valid numerical result. Recognising Brahmagupta's historical contribution does not mean accepting every rule in his writings as mathematically correct today.

Brahmagupta's place in Indian astronomy

Like Aryabhata, Brahmagupta combined mathematics with astronomy. His works dealt with calculations relating to planetary positions and eclipses. His distinctive place in the history of mathematics, however, is especially associated with the systematic treatment of zero and negative numbers.

Prelims focus

  • Decimal system: uses 10 digits, 0 to 9, with place values based on powers of 10.
  • Zero: acts both as a placeholder and as a number.
  • Brahmagupta: approximately 598–670 CE.
  • Brahmasphutasiddhanta: 628 CE.
  • Khandakhadyaka: 665 CE.
  • Trap: Brahmagupta formulated important rules for zero, but he was not the sole inventor of the decimal system.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, chapter 'Buildings, Paintings and Books', printed p. 131; University of St Andrews, MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Brahmagupta' and 'Zero', sections on the decimal system and arithmetic rules, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: How zero preserves the correct place value in 205.

title: The Decimal System, Zero and Brahmagupta's Mathematical Rules
